title: Shoe Co.
difficulty_source_label: Overall 1, Quant 2, Creativity 1 (1-3 scale); Quant Level - MEDIUM
fit_question: Tell me about a situation where you dealt with ambiguity. Alternatively, tell me about a time you motivated a diverse team.
prompt: Shoe Co. is a small affordable-luxury shoe retailer, branded as classic and fun, with an average price of $300 per pair. Same-store transaction volume is declining even as competitors' same-store sales grow. What is the root cause?

clarifying_info.answer: Sales volume can be understood as the average number of transactions within the store.

interviewer_notes: The case is labeled Market Entry in the source but is substantively a same-store-sales root-cause and investment case. Guide the candidate from market and customer hypotheses toward the three consumer-survey exhibits. Once product assortment is identified, provide that design spend is 6.5% of $800M sales versus an 8% benchmark, gross margin is 40%, and an expert expects getting assortment right to lift sales by 5-10%.

suggested_framework.summary: Locate where transactions are lost in the customer funnel, compare customer and competitor trends, diagnose the underlying product issue, and test the economics of fixing it.

tree.label: Explain Shoe Co.'s same-store transaction decline

children.label: Geography, category trends, competitor growth, and economic conditions
Awareness, visits, conversion, basket, repeat purchase, and returns
Design, assortment, quality, price, store experience, and brand fit
Design capability, spend, sales lift, margin, timing, and implementation risk

stages.interviewer_asks: How would you find the root cause?
stages.expected_answer: Because competitors are growing, test a client-specific problem. Segment same-store transactions into traffic, awareness, conversion, repeat purchase, and returns; examine customer demographics and preferences, product design/assortment, price, quality, and store experience; compare competitors and regions; then quantify the value and feasibility of remedies.
good_answer_signals: Focuses on root cause before solutions

stages.interviewer_asks: What does Exhibit 1 say about the funnel?
stages.expected_answer: Awareness is relatively high at about 70%, but only about 20% of aware consumers purchase, so the main leakage is conversion, not awareness. Nonbuyers cite style, store, product, and price issues, so further segment the persistent conversion problem.

stages.interviewer_asks: What does Exhibit 2 reveal about existing customers?
stages.expected_answer: Thirty percent report lower spending. Forty percent of that subgroup reduced product purchases; roughly three-quarters of those reasons are design-driven, so approximately 30% of consumers with decreased spend cite design-related purchase reduction (40% x 75%). The issue is persistent and linked to missed trends, stale designs, and changed styles more than a broad market decline.

About 40% of all respondents are familiar nonbuyers, and product reasons are the largest nonpurchase category at 40% of that group. Within product reasons, about 80% are product-specific, with design and quality smaller. Together the exhibits point to the wrong assortment and failure to match customer style trends as the central root cause.
good_answer_signals: Separates population shares from conditional reason shares
Identifies product as the largest conversion barrier

stages.interviewer_asks: What is the expected return from increasing design spend to the industry benchmark?
stages.info_to_release: Industry design spend is 8% of sales versus Shoe Co.'s 6.5%. Shoe Co. has $800M in sales and a 40% gross margin. An expert expects a 5-10% sales lift from getting assortment right.
stages.expected_answer: Incremental design spend is 1.5% x $800M=$12M. At the conservative 5% sales lift, incremental sales are $40M and gross profit is $16M, yielding $4M net annual contribution after the design investment. At 10%, sales lift is $80M, gross profit $32M, and net contribution $20M. The book uses the conservative $4M case.
good_answer_signals: Applies gross margin to incremental sales

stages.interviewer_asks: What else should Shoe Co. consider?
stages.expected_answer: Decide whether design should be built in-house or outsourced, whether $12M reaches minimum efficient scale, hiring and facility ramp-up costs, time to refresh assortment, payback and NPV, brand consistency, customer research, test-market design, and how to track conversion and repeat purchase.

Increase design investment toward the 8% benchmark and use consumer research to refresh assortment. High awareness but weak conversion, persistent purchase reductions, and product/design survey results point to a style mismatch. A $12M incremental investment yields about $4M net contribution at a conservative 5% sales lift and up to $20M at 10%. Pilot designs first, track conversion, and validate timing, capability, and cannibalization risks.

exhibits.title: Consumer awareness, purchase, and nonpurchase reasons
exhibits.description: Consumer funnel and stated reasons aware consumers do not purchase.

rows: Style, store, product, and price issues

exhibits.key_insight: Awareness is high, but conversion among aware consumers is only about 20%.

exhibits.title: Recent-purchaser spending changes and reasons
exhibits.description: Three-year spending trend and nested reasons for decreased purchasing.
exhibits.key_insight: Design-related reasons explain roughly 30% of reduced purchasing responses: 40% times about 75%.

exhibits.title: Familiarity and reasons for nonpurchase
exhibits.description: Familiarity funnel, nonpurchase causes, and detailed product drivers.
exhibits.key_insight: Product and assortment issues are the largest stated barrier among familiar nonbuyers.

math.question: How much additional design spend is required?
What is net annual contribution at a 5% sales lift?
What is net annual contribution at a 10% sales lift?

synthesis: Shoe Co.'s same-store transaction decline is primarily an assortment and design mismatch: awareness is high, conversion is weak, and both former purchasers and familiar nonbuyers point to product/style issues. Raise design spend from 6.5% to the 8% benchmark, a $12M investment. The conservative 5% sales lift yields $4M net annual contribution, with $20M at the 10% upper estimate. Pilot the assortment and monitor conversion before scaling.
what_great_looks_like: Calculates both conservative and upside returns
Connects pilot metrics to the diagnosis
common_pitfalls: Confusing percent of all customers with percent of a subgroup

low_confidence_fields: Exact percentages read from survey charts are approximate because several unlabeled segment boundaries must be inferred visually.
extraction.notes: All investment and sales-lift math was independently recomputed and matches the source. The source calls $4M a 'gross margin lift'; it is more precisely incremental gross profit after subtracting added design expense. Exhibit tables contain only chart inputs, with approximate labels where the source chart does not print exact percentages. Reviewed and accepted by Claude 2026-09-30.
